0.value:
mag_offset measures a magnetometer: it collects the field readings as the sensor is turned, fits a sphere to them, and tells you how far that sphere sits from the origin.

WHY THIS MATTERS:
An inertial sensor works out which way is down from gravity, and that is reliable. Which way is NORTH it takes from the magnetic field, and that is not: a bit of magnetised metal travelling with the sensor adds its own field to the earth's, and the sensor reads a heading that is wrong by an amount that depends on which way it is facing. The result is a limb turned about the vertical, which no downstream filtering will remove, because it is not noise.

WHAT THE SPHERE MEANS:
Turn a clean sensor through every orientation and its readings trace a sphere centred on the origin, with a radius equal to the strength of the field. A magnetised sensor traces the same sphere, moved off the origin - and that displacement is the hard-iron offset, the field the sensor carries with it.

So the fit gives you three things:
  centre     the hard-iron offset, x y z - what the sensor adds to every reading
  radius     the strength of the field the sensor is in
  residual   how far, on average, the readings sit from the fitted sphere - a
             measure of how well a sphere fits at all

READING THE NUMBERS:
Judge the offset by its length as a percentage of the radius. As a reference, a clean chest sensor in the 2026 studio assessments read a radius of 54.6 microtesla, an offset about 1.5 microtesla long (under 3 percent of the radius) and a residual of 0.42 microtesla. Clean sensors there ran from about 0.3 to 3 percent; the sensors that needed recalibrating carried 7 to 33 percent.

The radius should match the local earth field - about 54.5 microtesla in Toronto. A low radius usually means the sensor was not turned through enough orientations, not that the sensor's scale is wrong. A high residual with a small offset means either too little coverage again, or a distortion that is not a simple offset (soft iron).

A sensor with a large offset needs recalibrating in Shadow, not correcting in software.

HOW TO MEASURE A SENSOR:
Stay in one spot, waist height or higher, and turn the sensor slowly through as many orientations as you can - every face pointing every way. Do not walk around while you turn it, and do not do it near the floor: the field of the room itself varies from place to place, and moving through that variation while turning mixes it into a fit that assumes one field. (To map the room itself, do the opposite: keep one sensor in a fixed orientation and move it.)

COLLECTING:
Each reading arriving at 'magnetometer' is kept if it is at least 'min point spacing' away from the last one kept, so holding the sensor still does not pile up points in one place. Readings of exactly zero are ignored. Only the newest 'max points' are kept. The fit starts once there are 8 points, and every kept reading refits and sends everything again.

The units are whatever comes in; from shadow_sensor they are microtesla.

SYNTAX:
mag_offset

EXAMPLE:
mag_offset

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

magnetometer:
One reading, three numbers x y z - an array or a list.

clear:
Discard the collected readings and start again. Sends the empty result.

max points:
How many readings to keep, newest first. Default 2000.

offset (uT) / radius (uT) / fit residual / samples:
The current fit, and how many readings it is based on.

OPTIONS:

min point spacing:
How far a reading must be from the last one kept, in the units of the readings. Default 1.

OUTPUTS:

cloud:
All the kept readings, one row each.

centered cloud:
The same readings with the offset taken away - they should now sit on a sphere around the origin.

center:
The offset, x y z.

radius / residual:
The fit, as above.

RELATED:
shadow_sensor supplies the readings from a suit.
mgl_point_cloud can draw 'cloud' or 'centered cloud' in 3-D.
